events.title: Tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, tribune from 10 December 134, used the concilium plebis to pass an agrarian law over senatorial opposition, deposed a vetoing colleague, and sought immediate re-election. Ancient and modern writers alike treat the year as the start of the Republic's century of crisis.
events.detail: Tiberius was grandson of Scipio Africanus through his mother Cornelia and brother-in-law of Scipio Aemilianus. Plutarch preserves a story from Gaius' pamphlet that Tiberius conceived the law while travelling through Etruria to Numantia in 137 and seeing the land worked by imported slaves. His backers were heavyweights: Appius Claudius Pulcher (princeps senatus, his father-in-law), Publius Mucius Scaevola (consul 133) and Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus. The novelty lay less in the law than in the methods: bypassing the senate, removing a tribune, and claiming the Pergamene bequest for the people.
scholarship: Bernstein, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus: Tradition and Apostasy (1978)
events.debate: Was Tiberius a reformer responding to real rural depopulation (Brunt) or did he exaggerate a manpower crisis (Rich, Historia 1983)? Archaeological survey of the ager Romanus and Etruria does not show the wholesale disappearance of small farms that Appian and Plutarch imply.

events.title: Lex Sempronia agraria
events.summary: Tiberius Gracchus' land law enforced the old limit of 500 iugera on holdings of public land (ager publicus), with extra allowances for sons, and redistributed the surplus to poor citizens in small inalienable lots, administered by a three-man commission.
events.detail: The limit itself was old (attributed to the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367), but had long gone unenforced. Appian (BC 1.9-11) gives 500 iugera plus 250 for each of two sons; possessors kept the retained land rent-free in perpetuity. New allotments, perhaps of 30 iugera, paid a vectigal and could not be sold. The commissioners (tresviri agris iudicandis adsignandis) were Tiberius, his brother Gaius and Appius Claudius Pulcher; after 133 they continued working, and boundary stones naming the commissioners survive from Campania, Lucania and the Hirpini. The census rose from 318,823 (131/0) to 394,736 (125/4), which may reflect the distributions. Italian allies who occupied ager publicus lost land without gaining allotments, a grievance that fed straight into the citizenship question.
scholarship: Roselaar, Public Land in the Roman Republic (2010)
events.debate: Whether allies were entitled to allotments and how large the lots were is disputed; the law's text does not survive, and the later lex agraria of 111 (CIL I2 585) is the main documentary witness to its effects.

events.title: Deposition of the tribune Marcus Octavius
events.summary: When his colleague Marcus Octavius persistently vetoed the agrarian bill, Tiberius had the plebeian assembly vote him out of office, arguing that a tribune who acted against the people forfeited his office. It was without precedent.
events.detail: Appian and Plutarch describe the tribes voting in turn; when 17 of the 35 had voted for removal Tiberius paused and begged Octavius to relent, then completed the vote. Octavius was dragged from the rostra. Tiberius' argument that a tribune derived his authority from the people and could lose it was coherent popular theory, but to opponents it destroyed the veto, the main brake within the tribunate, and made the assembly's will unlimited.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Mass Oratory and Political Power in the Late Roman Republic (2004)

events.title: Murder of Tiberius Gracchus
events.summary: During the assembly to elect tribunes for 132, at which Tiberius sought re-election, the pontifex maximus Scipio Nasica led senators and their clients up the Capitol and clubbed Tiberius and some 300 supporters to death. The bodies were thrown into the Tiber.
events.detail: The consul Scaevola refused to act without legal process, so Nasica called on those who wished to save the state to follow him, his toga drawn over his head in priestly fashion. The weapons were broken benches and staves: no swords. This was the first political killing within the city in living memory and, as Appian notes, set the pattern for those that followed. In 132 the consuls Popillius Laenas and Rupilius ran a special court that executed or exiled Tiberius' associates; Nasica was sent on an embassy to Asia to remove him from popular anger and died at Pergamon.

events.title: Revolt of Aristonicus in Asia
events.summary: Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II, claimed the Attalid throne as Eumenes III and resisted the Roman inheritance, drawing on slaves and the rural poor whom he called Heliopolitai, citizens of the Sun.
events.detail: He minted cistophori in his regnal name, and Blossius of Cumae, Tiberius Gracchus' Stoic adviser, joined him. The utopian label rests on Strabo and Diodorus; modern scholars see him primarily as a dynastic pretender exploiting social discontent. He held out until 129.
events.debate: The Heliopolitai as a social-revolutionary programme versus a dynastic war is debated.

events.title: Battle of Leucae
events.summary: The consul Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus was defeated and killed by Aristonicus near Leucae. Captured, he provoked a Thracian guard into killing him rather than be paraded alive.

battle.significance: Demonstrated that the Asian inheritance would have to be conquered and delayed the province's organisation by two years.

events.title: Siege of Stratonicea and capture of Aristonicus
events.summary: Marcus Perperna (consul 130) besieged Aristonicus in Stratonicea and starved him into surrender. Aristonicus was taken to Rome and strangled in prison.

battle.significance: Ended Attalid resistance; Perperna died before his triumph and Manius Aquillius (consul 129) completed the settlement.

events.title: Organisation of the province of Asia
events.summary: Manius Aquillius and a ten-man senatorial commission organised the Attalid kingdom as the province of Asia, giving Phrygia to Mithridates V of Pontus and parts of Lycaonia to the sons of Ariarathes of Cappadocia. It became Rome's richest province.
events.detail: Aquillius' milestones (the earliest Roman road markers in Asia, in Latin and Greek) mark a road system radiating from Pergamon. The sale of Phrygia to Pontus was later alleged to have been bought with bribes, and Gaius Gracchus attacked it; the senate revoked the grant after Mithridates V's death in c. 120, a grievance Mithridates VI never forgot.

events.title: Lex Rupilia for Sicily
events.summary: After the slave war, Rupilius and a senatorial commission issued a charter (lex data) for Sicily, regulating which courts heard disputes between Sicilians, Romans and cities. Cicero still cites it in the Verrines sixty years later.

events.title: Lex Papiria tabellaria
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Papirius Carbo extended the written secret ballot to legislative assemblies, completing the series begun by the lex Gabinia (139, elections) and lex Cassia (137, trials).
events.detail: Cicero (De legibus 3.35) regarded the ballot laws as undermining aristocratic influence. Carbo also proposed allowing tribunes to stand for immediate re-election, which failed, opposed by Scipio Aemilianus.

events.title: Death of Scipio Aemilianus
events.summary: Scipio Aemilianus, who had taken up the Italian allies' complaints against the land commission and had the commission's judicial powers transferred to the consul, was found dead in bed the morning he was due to speak. No inquiry was held.
events.detail: Rumour accused his wife Sempronia (the Gracchi's sister), Cornelia, Carbo and Fulvius Flaccus. Natural death is quite possible. The episode marks the moment the agrarian question became an Italian question: allies who possessed ager publicus had no vote and could only appeal to Roman patrons.
events.debate: Murder or natural death; ancient authors themselves were divided.

events.title: Census registers 394,736 citizens
events.summary: The census of 125/4 counted 394,736 adult male citizens, up from 318,823 in 131/0. The jump of nearly a quarter is commonly linked to the Gracchan allotments, which required citizen status and may have encouraged poor men to register.
events.debate: Real population growth, better registration, or both? Brunt saw registration effects; the figures are also subject to textual corruption.

events.title: Lex Iunia expels non-citizens from Rome
events.summary: The tribune Marcus Iunius Pennus carried a law expelling non-citizens from the city, aimed at Italians who had come to lobby against the land commission. Gaius Gracchus spoke against it.

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus proposes citizenship for the allies
events.summary: The consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, a land commissioner, proposed giving allies citizenship or alternatively the right of appeal (provocatio). The senate side-stepped it by sending him to help Massalia against the Saluvii, which began the Roman conquest of southern Gaul.

events.title: Revolt and destruction of Fregellae
events.summary: Fregellae, the leading Latin colony on the Liris, revolted after Flaccus' bill failed. The praetor Lucius Opimius took it through the treachery of Quintus Numitorius Pullus and razed it; Fabrateria Nova was founded nearby in 124.
events.detail: Fregellae had been loyal through Hannibal's war. Excavation shows a prosperous town with Hellenistic houses and a sanctuary of Aesculapius abruptly destroyed. The revolt's isolation shows the allies were not yet ready for concerted action; its brutal suppression anticipated Opimius' role in 121.

battle.significance: First armed allied revolt over citizenship; a warning of the Social War three decades later.

events.note: Fregellae was a Latin colony; both sides are given as 'rome' because no separate polity is defined for it.

events.title: Metellus conquers the Balearic Islands
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus (consul 123) subdued the Balearic islanders, ostensibly for piracy, protecting his ships against their famous slingers with stretched hides, and settled 3,000 Romans from Iberia at Palma and Pollentia. He took the cognomen Balearicus.

events.title: Foundation of Aquae Sextiae
events.summary: Gaius Sextius Calvinus, having destroyed the Saluvian oppidum at Entremont, founded a Roman garrison post at the hot springs below it, the first permanent Roman settlement in Transalpine Gaul.
events.detail: Entremont, with its sculptures of heroes holding severed heads, was sacked c. 123; its destruction layer matches the literary record.

events.title: Tribunates of Gaius Gracchus
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus, tribune in 123 and 122, passed the most ambitious legislative programme of the Republic: subsidised grain, equestrian juries, Asian tax farming at Rome, protection of citizens from summary execution, colonies, roads and army reforms.
events.detail: Gaius was a better orator than his brother (Cicero thought him the most gifted of all) and turned to face the people in the Forum rather than the Curia. His laws created constituencies: the urban plebs (grain), the equites (juries and Asian contracts), soldiers (free clothing), contractors (roads, granaries). Re-elected for 122, he sailed to Africa for 70 days to found Junonia, during which the senate's tribune Livius Drusus outbid him. His citizenship bill failed and he lost the election for 121.
events.debate: Whether Gaius had a coherent plan to reshape the state (Mommsen) or reacted to events; the chronology of his laws between 123 and 122 is uncertain.

events.title: Lex Sempronia frumentaria
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus' grain law guaranteed every citizen in Rome a monthly ration of grain at 6 1/3 asses per modius, below the market price, and built public granaries. Every later popularis grain law built on it.
events.detail: The price was fixed, not free; Clodius made it free in 58. Cicero tells of the ex-consul Piso Frugi, an opponent, queueing for his ration because, he said, if Gracchus was distributing his property he wanted his share (Tusc. 3.48).

events.title: Gracchan jury law and the lex repetundarum
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus transferred the juries of the extortion court (quaestio de repetundis) from senators to equites. The surviving bronze law on extortion (Tabula Bembina, CIL I2 583), usually identified with the lex Acilia of 123/2, shows the details: 450 jurors, none of them senators, and generous rewards for successful prosecutors.
events.detail: Appian says the change made equites masters of the senate; governors now feared juries drawn from the business class that profited from provincial taxation. The control of the juries became the most fought-over question of the next fifty years: Caepio 106, Glaucia c. 101, Drusus 91, Sulla 81, Aurelius Cotta 70.
events.debate: Whether the lex Acilia is Gaius' own law or a colleague's, and whether Plutarch's version (adding equites to the senate) is a confusion with Drusus in 91.

events.title: Lex Sempronia on the taxes of Asia
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus ordered that the tithe of the new province of Asia be auctioned by the censors at Rome in large five-year contracts. This created the great companies of publicani whose interests shaped Roman policy in the East for a century.

events.title: Lex Sempronia de capite civis
events.summary: Gaius' law forbade capital sentences on citizens without the people's authorisation and made any magistrate who executed a citizen without trial liable to prosecution. Popillius Laenas, who had punished Tiberius' followers in 132, went into exile.
events.detail: The law framed the arguments of 121, 63 and 58: Opimius' defence in 120, Cicero's execution of the Catilinarians and his exile under the lex Clodia all turned on whether the senatus consultum ultimum overrode it.

events.title: Foundation of Colonia Junonia at Carthage
events.summary: Under the lex Rubria Gaius Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus founded a colony of 6,000 settlers on the site of Carthage, the first Roman colony outside Italy. Reports that wolves tore up the boundary markers were used against it, and the colony was formally abolished, though the allotments survived.
events.note: Settlers kept their land; the lex agraria of 111 deals with their holdings.

events.title: Livius Drusus outbids Gaius Gracchus
events.summary: With senatorial backing the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus proposed twelve colonies of 3,000 poor citizens each, the abolition of rent on Gracchan allotments and a ban on flogging Latin soldiers. The colonies were never founded, but the proposals drained Gaius' support.

events.title: Gaius Gracchus' citizenship bill defeated
events.summary: Gaius proposed full citizenship for Latins and Latin rights for other Italian allies. The consul Fannius asked the plebs whether, if they gave the Latins the vote, they expected to find room at the games and festivals, and the bill failed.
events.debate: Appian and Plutarch differ on the scope; the bill's failure showed that the Roman plebs would not share its privileges.

events.title: First senatus consultum ultimum
events.summary: After a supporter of Gaius killed the consul Opimius' attendant Quintus Antyllius, the senate decreed that the consul should see that the state suffered no harm (videret consul ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet). Opimius used it as authority to attack the Gracchans on the Aventine.
events.detail: This was the first use of the decree modern scholars call the senatus consultum ultimum. It conferred no new legal power; it signalled senatorial backing for force and a promise to defend the magistrate afterwards. It was used again in 100, 88/83, 77, 63, 62, 52, 49, 48, 47 and 43. Whether it could override the citizen's right of appeal was never resolved.
scholarship: Lintott, The Constitution of the Roman Republic (1999)

events.title: Death of Gaius Gracchus and the Aventine massacre
events.summary: Opimius, with senators, equites and Cretan archers, stormed the Aventine where Fulvius Flaccus had occupied the temple of Diana. Flaccus and his son were killed; Gaius fled across the Tiber and had his slave Philocrates kill him in the grove of Furrina. Some 3,000 followers were executed afterwards.
events.detail: Opimius had offered Gaius' head's weight in gold; Plutarch says the man who brought it had filled it with lead and it weighed 17 2/3 pounds. Opimius then rebuilt the temple of Concord, and someone carved beneath the dedication that a work of madness had made a temple of Concord. The Gracchi became martyrs: Plutarch says the people set up statues to them and offered sacrifices at the places of their deaths.

events.title: Opimius restores the temple of Concord
events.summary: By senatorial decree Opimius rebuilt the temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol and added the Basilica Opimia beside it. The graffito 'Vecordiae opus aedem facit Concordiae' summed up popular opinion.
events.detail: The temple later hosted the senate meeting of 5 December 63 that condemned the Catilinarians.

events.title: Battle of Vindalium
events.summary: The proconsul Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus defeated the Allobroges at Vindalium, where the Sulga (Sorgue) meets the Rhône. His elephants panicked the Gallic horses; 20,000 Gauls were said to have been killed.
events.detail: Suetonius (Nero 2) says Ahenobarbus afterwards rode through the province on an elephant escorted by his troops, a scene of triumphal display remembered in his family.
events.locName: Confluence of the Sorgue and Rhône

battle.significance: Broke the Allobroges and opened the Rhône corridor to Roman control.

events.title: Battle of the Isara
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus, grandson of Aemilius Paullus, crushed a huge army of Arverni and Allobroges under the Arvernian king Bituitus near the Isère. Bituitus, famous for his silver chariot and hounds, was later seized at a parley by Ahenobarbus and interned at Alba Fucens.
events.detail: Ancient totals of 120,000 to 130,000 Gauls killed against 15 Roman dead are fantastical, but the victory ended Arvernian hegemony in southern Gaul. Fabius took the name Allobrogicus and, with Ahenobarbus, set up stone trophy towers on the battlefields, a novelty Florus remarks on.
events.locName: Confluence of the Isère and Rhône

battle.significance: Destroyed the Arvernian hegemony and led directly to the creation of the province of Transalpine Gaul.

events.title: Trial and acquittal of Opimius
events.summary: Prosecuted before the people for killing citizens without trial, Opimius argued that the senate's decree justified him and was acquitted. His defender was Gaius Papirius Carbo, once a Gracchan ally, now consul.
events.detail: The acquittal gave the senatus consultum ultimum practical force. Opimius was convicted in 109 by the Mamilian commission for taking Jugurtha's bribes and died in exile at Dyrrachium.

events.title: Marius' tribunate and the lex Maria
events.summary: As tribune Gaius Marius passed a law narrowing the gangways (pontes) by which voters passed to cast their ballots, to prevent aristocrats from inspecting votes, and threatened to have the consul Cotta arrested when the senate opposed it. He then surprised everyone by vetoing a grain bill.

events.title: Foundation of Narbo Martius
events.summary: A citizen colony was founded at Narbo, championed by the young orator Lucius Licinius Crassus against senatorial objection. It anchored the new province of Transalpine Gaul and the road to Spain.
events.detail: Narbo was the first citizen colony outside Italy that survived (Junonia having been abolished). The Via Domitia, built by Ahenobarbus, ran through it; a milestone naming Gnaeus Domitius as imperator, found at Treilles near Narbonne, is the oldest Roman milestone known in Gaul.

events.title: Construction of the Via Domitia
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus built the road linking Italy to Spain along the Mediterranean coast of Gaul, from the Alps via Nemausus and Narbo to the Pyrenees. Pompey later fortified its Pyrenean pass with his trophies (71).
events.note: Date of construction c. 120-118; Cicero mentions its upkeep in the 70s.

events.title: Death of Micipsa and partition of Numidia
events.summary: King Micipsa, son of Masinissa, left Numidia jointly to his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal and to his adopted nephew Jugurtha, a veteran of Numantia with friends among the Roman nobility. Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered at Thirmida within a year.
events.detail: In 116 a senatorial commission led by Opimius divided the kingdom: Jugurtha got the richer, more populous west; Adherbal the east with Cirta and its ports. Sallust says the commissioners were bought.

events.title: Trial of the Vestals and human sacrifice in the Forum Boarium
events.summary: After a prodigy in which a girl riding on horseback was struck dead by lightning, three Vestals, Aemilia, Licinia and Marcia, were accused of unchastity. The pontiffs condemned only Aemilia; a special tribunal under Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla condemned the other two in 113. Two Gauls and two Greeks were buried alive in the Forum Boarium, and a temple was vowed to Venus Verticordia.
events.detail: This was the last recorded Roman human sacrifice of this ritual type (also performed in 228 and 216). Cassius was the judge famous for asking 'cui bono?'. The affair shows religious anxiety about the Cimbri and the political use of religious courts: the tribunal was set up by a tribune's law over pontifical jurisdiction.

events.title: Battle of Noreia
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, trying to protect the Taurisci of Noricum, Roman guest-friends, ambushed the migrating Cimbri after negotiating their withdrawal, and was routed. Only a storm saved his army from annihilation.
events.detail: This was the first Roman encounter with the Cimbri, a people whose origin the ancients placed in Jutland. Carbo was later prosecuted by Marcus Antonius and killed himself. Noreia's site is unknown; the Magdalensberg and sites near Neumarkt in Styria have been proposed.

battle.significance: Opened twelve years of Cimbrian warfare and exposed Roman treachery as counterproductive.

events.title: Siege of Cirta and the massacre of the Italians
events.summary: Jugurtha besieged Adherbal in Cirta for months while senatorial embassies came and went. The Italian traders defending the city persuaded Adherbal to surrender on terms; Jugurtha tortured him to death and massacred the adult Numidians and Italian merchants (negotiatores) alike.
events.detail: The killing of Italici, men with links to the equestrian business class, made war unavoidable: the tribune-elect Gaius Memmius whipped up the people and the senate assigned Numidia to the consul of 111, Bestia.

battle.significance: Turned a dynastic dispute into a Roman war.

events.note: Both sides are Numidian; Adherbal's faction is given as numidia.

events.title: Jugurtha in Rome and the murder of Massiva
events.summary: After Bestia granted Jugurtha lenient terms, the tribune Memmius summoned him to Rome under safe conduct to testify against the nobles he had bribed. Another tribune, Baebius, forbade him to speak. While in Rome Jugurtha had his cousin Massiva, a rival claimant, assassinated by his agent Bomilcar and was expelled.
events.detail: Leaving the city, Jugurtha is said to have looked back and called Rome a city for sale and doomed to perish if it found a buyer. Sallust built his whole monograph around this theme of aristocratic venality.
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

events.title: Lex agraria of 111
events.summary: An agrarian law, preserved on the reverse of the bronze Tabula Bembina (CIL I2 585), converted Gracchan allotments and permitted holdings of ager publicus into private land free of rent and halted further distribution. It effectively wound up the Gracchan programme in Italy and regulated public land in Africa and at Corinth.
events.detail: It is the longest surviving Republican statute text. Appian's account (BC 1.27) of three post-Gracchan laws, first allowing sale of allotments, then stopping distribution, then abolishing rent, is usually reconciled with it.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

events.title: Capitulation of Aulus Albinus at Suthul
events.summary: Aulus Postumius Albinus, left in command by his brother the consul, marched in midwinter to seize Jugurtha's treasury at Suthul. A night attack, helped by bribed centurions and auxiliaries, broke his camp; the army passed under the yoke and agreed to leave Numidia within ten days.
events.detail: The senate repudiated the agreement. The humiliation produced the Mamilian commission and, indirectly, Marius' consulship.

sides.losses: camp taken, army sent under the yoke

battle.significance: The low point of the war; discredited the senatorial leadership at Rome.

events.note: Suthul is sometimes identified with Calama (Guelma).

events.title: The Mamilian commission
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Mamilius Limetanus established a special court, with equestrian juries, to try those who had taken Jugurtha's money. It condemned Opimius, Bestia, Spurius Albinus, Gaius Cato and the priest Gaius Sulpicius Galba. Scaurus, himself implicated, contrived to be one of the three presiding commissioners.

events.title: Battle of the Muthul
events.summary: Jugurtha ambushed Quintus Caecilius Metellus' column from a scrub-covered ridge parallel to its march. After a long day's fighting the Romans drove off the Numidian infantry while Publius Rutilius Rufus defeated Bomilcar's elephants, killing or capturing all 44.
events.detail: Sallust's set-piece is the best tactical narrative of the war. The battle showed Metellus' disciplined army could beat Jugurtha in the open but not catch him; Jugurtha simply dispersed and reassembled.

sides.strength: consular army of perhaps 2 legions plus allies

battle.significance: Tactical Roman success that did not end the war; Jugurtha turned to guerrilla warfare.

events.title: Failed siege of Zama
events.summary: Metellus besieged Zama to force Jugurtha to battle but failed to take it and withdrew to winter quarters. Over the winter the garrison at Vaga was massacred in a rising, and its commander Turpilius, a friend of Metellus, was executed.

battle.significance: Showed the limits of siege warfare against a mobile enemy.

events.title: Scaurus builds the Pons Mulvius and Via Aemilia Scauri
events.summary: As censor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus rebuilt the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber in stone and built the Via Aemilia Scauri along the Tyrrhenian coast from Pisa via Vada to Dertona. The bridge's piers still carry traffic.

events.title: Siege of Thala
events.summary: Metellus marched across waterless country, carrying water in skins on pack animals, and took Jugurtha's treasure town Thala after a 40-day siege. Jugurtha escaped with his children and much of the treasure; Roman deserters inside burned themselves in the palace.

battle.significance: Showed Rome could reach Jugurtha's strongholds; prompted Bocchus of Mauretania to join Jugurtha.

events.title: Marius elected consul for 107
events.summary: Gaius Marius, a novus homo from Arpinum and Metellus' legate, returned to Rome against his commander's wishes, campaigned on Metellus' slowness and was elected consul. A tribunician law then gave him the Numidian command, overriding the senate's decision to prorogue Metellus.
events.detail: Metellus had told him not to hurry: he could stand when Metellus' son did, a jibe at a man of nearly fifty. Sallust stresses the support of equites and Italian businessmen frustrated by the war's cost. The popular reassignment of a command against the senate's allocation was a precedent repeated in 88 with fatal results.

events.title: Marius enrols the capite censi
events.summary: Raising reinforcements for Numidia, Marius enrolled volunteers from the proletarii (capite censi, those assessed by head count) rather than conscripting from the property classes. Sallust says he did it to court popularity or because the poor had nothing to lose.
events.detail: This is the core of what modern textbooks call the Marian reforms, a bundle that also includes the modification of the pilum with a wooden rivet (Plut Mar 25), the eagle as the legion's sole standard (Pliny NH 10.16, dated to his second consulship, 104), the soldier carrying his own kit (Marius' mules) and the cohort as tactical unit. The property qualification had been falling for a century (Polybius' 400 drachmae, later 1,500 or 4,000 asses), the cohort appears already in Polybius' Spanish narratives, and conscription continued after 107. The real change was a gradual one: armies of poor long-service men dependent on their general for discharge bounties of land.
scholarship: Gabba, Republican Rome: The Army and the Allies (1976)
Matthew, On the Wings of Eagles: The Reforms of Gaius Marius (2010)
events.debate: Gabba saw a decisive proletarianisation; Rich and Cadiou argue the 'Marian reforms' are largely a modern construct, the army changing gradually and recruitment of the poor being neither new nor universal after 107.

events.title: Defeat of Cassius Longinus by the Tigurini
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cassius Longinus, Marius' colleague, was killed with his legate Lucius Piso in an ambush by the Tigurini, a Helvetian canton, led by the young Divico. The legate Gaius Popillius Laenas saved the survivors by surrendering half the baggage and sending the army under the yoke.
events.detail: Caesar used the memory in 58 to justify attacking the Tigurini on the Arar, noting with satisfaction that the canton that had killed Lucius Piso, his father-in-law's grandfather, was the first to pay. Popillius was prosecuted for the surrender.
events.locName: territory of the Nitiobriges, near Agen

sides.losses: consul and legate killed; army under the yoke

battle.significance: Another consular army lost; the Volcae Tectosages of Tolosa defected.

events.note: Orosius places it near Burdigala; Livy's Periocha says in the territory of the Nitiobriges (Agen).

events.title: Marius takes Capsa
events.summary: Marius marched for days across desert, driving cattle for food and water, and stormed Capsa at dawn. Though it surrendered, the town was burned, its adult men killed and the rest sold, the booty divided among the troops.
events.detail: Sallust admits the act was contrary to the laws of war, justified as necessary against a fickle and hostile population. The exploit established Marius' reputation and his soldiers' loyalty.

battle.significance: Bold deep raid that demonstrated no Numidian town was beyond reach.

events.title: Capture of the fort on the Mulucha
events.summary: On the far western border of Numidia Marius besieged a fort on a sheer rock holding a royal treasury. A Ligurian auxiliary, climbing to gather snails, found a route up the back; a small party with trumpeters scaled it and panicked the defenders.

battle.significance: Deprived Jugurtha of treasure on the Mauretanian border, pressuring Bocchus.

events.title: Battles near Cirta
events.summary: Returning east to winter quarters, Marius' army was attacked at dusk by Jugurtha and Bocchus combined and held a pair of hills through the night; a dawn sally routed the Africans. A few days later a second battle near Cirta, with Sulla commanding the cavalry, ended in another Roman victory.
events.detail: Sallust describes Jugurtha in the second fight brandishing a bloody sword and shouting in Latin that he had killed Marius. After this Bocchus opened negotiations through Sulla.

sides.strength: large combined Numidian and Moorish cavalry and infantry

battle.significance: Broke the Numidian-Mauretanian alliance militarily and led Bocchus to betray Jugurtha.

events.title: Lex Servilia Caepionis
events.summary: The consul Quintus Servilius Caepio carried a law restoring senators to the extortion juries, alone or alongside equites. Crassus the orator's speech for it (attacking equestrian juries) was a celebrated model. It was reversed within a few years by Glaucia's law.
events.debate: Whether juries were wholly senatorial or mixed is uncertain.

events.title: The gold of Tolosa
events.summary: Caepio occupied Tolosa, whose Volcae Tectosages had joined the Cimbri, and seized temple treasures and sacred lakes of bullion that Posidonius put at 15,000 talents. The convoy sent to Massalia was ambushed and the treasure vanished; Caepio was widely suspected, and 'having Tolosan gold' became a proverb for ill-gotten wealth that brings ruin.
events.detail: Strabo, following Posidonius, rejects the legend that it was Delphic gold looted by Brennus' Gauls in 279. Caepio was condemned in 103 by a quaestio set up by the tribune Norbanus, partly over the treasure, partly over Arausio, and died in exile at Smyrna.

events.title: Bocchus hands Jugurtha to Sulla
events.summary: After months of secret negotiation, Bocchus of Mauretania lured Jugurtha to a meeting and handed him in chains to Marius' quaestor, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, ending the war. Bocchus received the western part of Numidia.
events.detail: Sulla had a signet ring cut showing the surrender and used it all his life; Marius regarded the credit as his own. In 91 Bocchus set up a gilded group of the scene on the Capitol, which provoked a near-riot between Marius' and Sulla's partisans. Sulla's son Faustus struck a denarius of it in 56 (RRC 426/1). Jugurtha walked in Marius' triumph on 1 January 104 and was then starved to death in the Tullianum.

events.title: Marius' Numidian triumph and death of Jugurtha
events.summary: Marius celebrated his triumph over Jugurtha on the day he entered his second consulship, then entered the senate still in triumphal dress, a breach of custom. Jugurtha was thrown naked into the Tullianum; Plutarch has him exclaim how cold the Romans' bath was before he starved six days later.
